newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AACHEN MUNICH.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - AACHEN MUNICH.

text.p: Wolfgang Kaske, chief executive of Germany's second largest insurer Aachen Munich, gave an unusual presentation at yesterday's press conference.

In addition to explaining the excellent 1996 figures, Kaske covered a time span of six years to chart the group's development. Kaske will retire at the end of the year, the new chief executive officer will be Hans Jaeger, currently head of group member Volksfuersorge.

Just before he withdraws from the scene, Kaske is presenting an account of his work. He and his management colleages are convinced that they stabilised AMB, which had been on a rocky course for some time. The AMB chief reminded the world of the strong growth - from 8.8 billion marks turnover in 1991 to a 20.0 billion turnover in 1997, accompanied by equally convincing increases in profits.

He explained how AMB managed to disentangle itself from the fate of the troubled BfG Bank by selling its majority to Credit Lyonnais. Kaske pointed to the consequences of the unsuccessful takeover attempt by French insurer AGF, which was finally blocked in 1992 by a German alliance of shareholders led by Allianz. And he proudly recalled the takeover of Volksfuersorge in 1993 and the present group restructuring.
Kaske's message is simple: his house is in order. Whatever follows, he has done his job well. That message was addressed to the public, but in particular to present and future shareholders.

The AMB management is well aware that the current ownership structure cannot be maintained. French shareholder AGF is unhappy with its 33.5 percent -- it either wants the majority or it wants a way to get out. Other shareholders, too, are looking for the exit door, while the share price is as high as it is now. This includes shareholders who bought AMB stock as part of the Allianz-organised defence against the AGF takeover.

Thus, turbulent times are looming with regard to the AMB group's owners. The task now facing AMB is to prevent this potential turmoil from spilling into the group and disturbing the current consolidation.

This is the real reason why Kaske made his remarks. He and Hans Jaeger both know that their work is far from complete. Integrating two groups as different as Aachener und Muenchener and Volksfuersorge, in order to create one stable, strong combination which gains market share rather than losing it, is a complicated job which will take years.
